data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism contains an internal contradiction: it describes corroboration as merely 'a report of past performance' carrying no inductive inference that the future will resemble the past, yet simultaneously asserts that 'acting on the best-tested theory is the only rational strategy to approximate truth.' If corroboration is purely retrospective and carries no forward-looking import (as the target insists by denying induction), then there is no rational basis on which it could be 'the only rational strategy' for future action — all strategies would be equally (un)justified. The claim that one particular strategy is uniquely rational presupposes that past testing results bear some positive relevance to future truth-approximation, which is precisely the inductive bridge the target claims to avoid. The target thus smuggles in induction not through the concept of verisimilitude (as prior objections noted) but through the normative force of its own methodological rule: calling a preference 'the only rational strategy' while denying it any predictive basis is self-undermining, since rationality of choice requires forward-looking justification, and a mere 'report of past performance' provides none without induction.
